Personalized Diagnosis of Chronic Cough If the patient’s medical history, physical examination and basic diagnostic tests are not conclusive, further diagnostic measures are indicated. A complete implementation of all possible technical tests listed above is not practicable. Therefore, a further, possibly interdisciplinary investigation [ ] in the sense of personalized medicine should be carried out. If the upper airways are suspected (“upper airways cough syndrome”) causing the chronic cough, extended diagnostic workup is indicated in this area. Chronic rhinosinusitis with or without polyps or PND should be ruled out by means of anterior and posterior rhinoscopy. A simple oral cavity inspection with the finding of mucus tracks on the posterior pharyngeal wall can also provide indications of upper airway involvement. Further diagnostics consist of performing a CT or MRI scan of the paranasal sinuses (S2k guideline on rhinosinusitis, AWMF guideline register). Laryngopharyngoscopy completes the ENT examination, checking for swelling and inflammation, particularly of the posterior parts of the larynx. If functional irritation of the larynx is suspected, a phoniatric examination may be useful. If allergic rhinitis or allergic asthma is suspected, an evaluation with prick testing, determination of the differential blood count and, if necessary, determination of total IgE and specific IgE should be performed. Specific provocation tests are seldom necessary. The respiratory workup includes pulmonary function testing with FeNO measurement (also relevant for NAEB [ ]), a unspecific bronchial provocation test, e.g., with metacholine, and the collection of blood, sputum and bronchial samples for further diagnosis [ , ]. Alternatively, a 4-week ex juvantibus therapy with a medium- or high-dose ICS/LABA combination is possible, if there is reasonable suspicion of cough-variant asthma (e.g., predominantly nocturnal or exertion-induced cough, elevated Th2 biomarkers (blood eosinophilia, FeNO)) [ , , ]. Chronic cough in the presence of classic GERD symptoms (heartburn, regurgitation) should be treated ex juvantibus with twice the standard dose of PPI for up to 90 days (see question 8). If there is no response, in justified individual cases complete gastroenterological workup, i.e., endoscopy, impedance pH probe, esophageal manometry should be performed. This also applies to clinically justifiable individual cases without classic GERD symptoms. Causality between cough and reflux can only be assumed if the SAP (symptom association probability) is 95% or higher (see question 8). In the case of chronic cough with sputum, the first step after basic diagnostics should be a microbiological sputum examination (including mycobacteria), followed by a CT scan of the thorax without contrast medium with 1 mm reconstructions. Bronchiectasis can be detected (see guidelines of the German Respiratory Society for bronchiectasis ( https://register.awmf.org/de/leitlinien/detail/020-030 ) as well as other diseases that are not evident on the chest X-ray, i.e., occult tumor, ILD, emphysema, etc. If the personalized diagnostic algorithm has remained inconclusive, a CT chest examination and, if there is clinical suspicion (e.g., of tracheobronchomalacia [ ], mucus plugging [ ], chronic infection, occult tumor) a bronchoscopy is also recommended. A cardiological investigation should be carried out if, despite a negative basic diagnosis of chronic cough, a cardiac cause (e.g., occult pulmonary congestion during exercise, arrhythmia, valvular heart diseases) appears possible in the context of the personalized assessment of the patient (see NVL Chronic Heart Failure, https://register.awmf.org/de/leitlinien/detail/nvl-006 ). Chapter 12 – Background Information on Key Question 12: Cough Therapy Respiratory Physiotherapy Productive Cough Respiratory physiotherapy in patients with secretion retention, impaired mucociliary clearance, and impaired cough clearance aims to improve secretion elimination and reduce symptoms. Techniques that support secretolysis, mobilization, transport, and secretion elimination by opening airways can reduce cough, the amount of sputum and significantly improve quality of life and cough-related symptoms [ , , ]. Active cycle of breathing techniques, secretion-promoting techniques including autogenous drainage, coughing techniques, positioning, vibration, and percussion can be supplemented with devices, inhalation, positive expiratory pressure devices with/without oscillations, high-frequency chest wall compression devices and air-stacking. In the case of a peak cough flow <160 L/min (measurable when coughing into a simple peak flow meter) and severely weakened patients, the cough should be assisted manually or with equipment [ ]. An up-to-date overview of the non-pharmacological treatment options for coughing described below can be found in the work by Peng et al. [ ]. Dry “Chesty” Cough The respiratory physiotherapy treatment of patients with dry irritating cough, such as RCC/UCC, aims to control cough to prevent or reduce the high symptom burden. This includes education on chronic cough including recognizing trigger factors, restoring physiological breathing patterns including nasal breathing and diaphragmatic breathing as well as techniques for cough irritation avoidance, cough prevention and cough attenuation [ , – ]. A review with 5 studies and 157 included patients found an improvement in cough-related quality of life, a significant reduction in cough frequency and a decrease in cough reflex sensitivity [ ]. Many years of clinical expert experience point to the great importance of patient education. A perceived cough stimulus (urge to cough) does not necessarily have to be answered with a subsequent cough. Speech Therapy Laryngeal Hypersensitivity and Coughing The speech therapy of coughing [ – ] and ILO (former terminology VCD) is based on the speech therapist's and medical diagnostic results. Usually, it consists of the following components: Speech therapist’s diagnostics includes symptom assessment of the cough and detection of functional imbalances of the larynx, vocal function, and swallowing. To clarify the role of the larynx, the questionnaire by Vertigan et al. [ ] is recommended. The consequent speech therapy includes the following components: - Psychoeducation: conveying the patient that the cough is not “imaginary”, promoting motivation and adherence, development of realistic treatment goals. - Counseling and initiation of measures, e.g., for voice hygiene; development of adapted suppression techniques and adapted coughing behavior with less subglottic pressure. - Advice on voice-damaging noxious substances and typical laryngeal stimuli, e.g., alcohol, reflux, dehydration [ ]. - Evaluation of the above-mentioned Vertigan questionnaire. - Offering and training of breathing techniques. - Adapted elements from the voice therapy. Speech therapy for chronic cough can be prescribed in accordance with the guidelines for diagnosis and treatment of voice function disorders https://register.awmf.org/de/leitlinien/detail/049-008 , SC2 “Swallowing disorders’ and SP6 “speech motor disorders”, if necessary, with patient-specific leading symptoms. Drug Therapy Most importantly, the disease underlying the symptom cough should be treated in accordance with the respective guidelines, i.e., causal treatments should be prescribed. For acute and subacute cough, evidence-based herbal and synthetic secretomotor drugs and antitussives are approved as symptomatic therapy for a treatment period of approximately 4 weeks. There is scientific evidence for their efficacy [ ]; see also key question 2. They may relieve and shorten the cough duration in the common cold. Their prescription is “off label” for chronic cough. If the cough does not occur as a symptom but as a disease on its own (RCC and UCC), secretomotor and antitussive drugs (see key question 2) can be prescribed intermittently for a limited period of time. These medications are not approved for long-term treatment of chronic cough. Gefapixant [ ], a P2X3 receptor antagonist, has been approved in Germany in a dosage of 45 mg bid for the treatment of RCC/UCC since September 2023. It is marketed in Austria, Switzerland, Norway, etc., but not in Germany. RCC and UCC are considered hypersensitivity (“neuropathy”) of the cough reflex. Dihydrocodeine is not recommended as it is metabolized in the body to an unpredictable extent to morphine and acts as such. The correct dosage is therefore difficult to determine. Future Therapies Chronic cough is not a uniform clinical entity [ ], and the efficacy of future drugs depends on the phenotype. For example, partial opioid µ and κ receptor agonists/antagonists work well in pulmonary fibrosis, for which there is recently published evidence available [ , ]. Cough triggered from the upper airways appears to respond to local osmotic rehydration therapy; a phase 3 trial is in preparation [ ]. Camlipixant, another P2X3 receptor antagonist, is in a phase 3 clinical trial, and other cough therapeutics are in development, including the neurokinin receptor antagonist orvepitant, a sodium channel NaV1.7 blocker, and others. The studies use both objective (24-h cough frequency) endpoints and patient-reported outcomes. By the end of the decade, several anti-cough drugs are expected to reach market maturity.
